scenes.narration: [serious] A love letter email broke millions of computers in 2000.
On May 4, 2000, an email arrived. The title said I LOVE YOU. It had a letter attached.
But it was not love. When you opened it, it sent itself to everyone you knew.
Then it erased photos and music. Email systems jammed around the world.
The damage cost billions of dollars.
The trail led to a student in Manila, Onel de Guzman. His school had rejected his project. It stole passwords.
But the Philippines had no law against hacking yet. So the charges were dropped. The love letter went unpunished.

facts.claim: The virus was released May 4, 2000, sent to about 84 million users, and 2.5 to 3 million were affected; analysts estimated $8.7 billion in damage
The email subject was ILOVEYOU and the attachment LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT was really a Visual Basic script; it emailed itself to every Outlook contact and overwrote files including JPEG and MP3
Damage was estimated at up to $10 billion; de Guzman's rejected thesis proposal was a program to steal internet passwords

Onel de Guzman, 23, a former student of a Manila computer college, was charged June 29, 2000; charges were dropped August 21, 2000 because existing laws did not cover hacking and the new law could not be applied retroactively
The Philippines had no law covering this kind of computer crime until June 2000; prosecutors dropped all charges

seo.title: ILOVEYOU Virus: The Love Letter That Infected Millions
seo.description: In May 2000 an email titled ILOVEYOU spread to millions of computers and wiped files worldwide. The suspect, a Manila student, walked free because no law covered hacking. Learn how the ILOVEYOU virus spread in 2000 and why its creator was not prosecuted. #cybersecurity #iloveyou #computervirus #shorts
